01.r: Points forward to the rule that follows.

02.r: How the remission works in practice.
02.n: The noun usually means 'word' or 'thing'; here, 'the matter of the remission', its terms. Hebrew has no 'is': the clause is verbless.

03.r: The seventh-year letting go of claims, named in the verse before.
03.n: BDB: a letting drop of exactions. Gesenius gives remission, release, citing this verse.

04.r: The lender is to let his claim drop.
04.n: An infinitive absolute used as a command, standing first in the clause. BDB gives 'let drop'; Gesenius gives a first sense to strike, to cast or throw down, from which comes letting something fall. We use 'remit' so that the verb and the noun 'remission' stay visibly one word in our English.

06.r: The one who holds the loan: the creditor.
06.n: Gesenius gives lord, master, possessor, owner; the brief's lexicon notes it is used as a noun of relation, 'master of' something. 'Owner of a loan' is a creditor, as most translations put it. Our brief tags this word as standing alone, which would make 'the loan of his hand' the thing remitted; the sense is the same either way.

07.r: The sum or goods lent out.
07.n: The brief records this noun in this one verse only. Gesenius gives 'a debt', from the verb 'lend' later in the verse; the brief's lexicon gives 'loan', of a loan released in the seventh year.

08.r: The lender's own hand, which made the loan.
08.n: 'The loan of his hand' is the loan he himself made. YLT takes 'his hand' as what is released: 'to release his hand'.

10.r: The lending that created the claim.
10.n: Gesenius gives first 'to borrow', then 'to lend to' someone, with 'to' written as in this verse. The imperfect can be 'lends' or 'has lent'.

11.n: The brief's lexicon gives friend, companion, fellow, and in a weaker sense another person. YLT reads the preposition as 'against his neighbour'.

13.r: He may not push the borrower for repayment.
13.n: Gesenius gives the base sense to impel, to urge, to drive, as a taskmaster drives a labourer, and cites this verse for urging a debtor, demanding a debt. The same verb's participle means a taskmaster or exactor of tribute.

14.r: Marks 'his neighbour' as the object of 'press'.
14.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'his neighbour'.

16.r: Adds 'his brother' as a second object.
16.n: 'And' with the object marker, which has no English equivalent; counted here with 'and his brother'.

17.r: The borrower seen as a fellow Israelite, a member of the same family of tribes.
17.n: The brief's lexicon lists brother, relative, and one of the same tribe; BDB adds 'relative'. Here it most likely means a fellow Israelite; that is a reading of the context.

18.r: Gives the reason the claim cannot be pressed.

19.r: The remission has been publicly announced.
19.n: Literally 'he has proclaimed' or 'one has proclaimed': an active verb with no named subject, which Hebrew often uses where English says 'has been'. YLT keeps it active, 'hath proclaimed'. Gesenius gives the first sense as to cry out, to call.

21.r: The remission belongs to the LORD and is kept for him.
21.n: Literally 'to the LORD'. Most translations make it possessive, 'the LORD's release'; YLT keeps 'to Jehovah'.

02.n: πρόσταγμα, 'ordinance, command': 'the ordinance of the release'.

03.n: ἄφεσις, 'release', as in the verse before.

04.n: Dictionary form supplied by hand: the brief gives none. ἀφήσεις, 'you shall release': the Greek turns the law to 'you'. ἀφίημι is the New Testament's verb for forgiving.

08.n: ἴδιον, 'one's own': 'every debt of your own'. Pairing it with 'his hand' is our reading of how the Greek reshapes the phrase.

10.n: ὀφείλει σοι, 'owes you': the Greek states the loan from the borrower's side, 'which your neighbour owes you'.

11.n: ὁ πλησίον, 'the neighbour', here the subject of 'owes'. The Greek names the neighbour once only, and has nothing for the second 'his neighbour'.

18.n: Dictionary form supplied by hand: the brief gives none.

19.n: ἐπικαλέω, 'to call upon, to call by name': ἐπικέκληται, 'has been called'.

21.n: The Greek adds 'your God': 'to the Lord your God'. τῳ θεῶ in our Greek text is τῷ θεῷ with its accents misread.
